sections.heading: Predict
sections.plan: Two prompts, each ending with '?'. Predict 1 (gist trap, marked <!-- gist-trap -->): a stem asks for the MOST cost-effective solution; two options meet every requirement and a third option is cheaper but misses one requirement. Which one is the answer? (The gist says: the cheapest.) Predict 2: of the 65 questions on the exam, how many count toward your score? Answers appear only in the Check reveals (U4).

sections.heading: What the exam measures
sections.plan: At most 250 words. One sentence: the exam (exam-name-and-code) validates design on the AWS Well-Architected Framework. Then one two-column table 'Exam fact | Value' (rows: questions 65, of them 50 scored and 15 unscored that you cannot identify; 130 minutes; ESL +30 for non-native English speakers; passing score 720 on a scale of 100 to 1,000; scored content by domain 30 / 26 / 24 / 20 percent; retake after a fail: 14 calendar days; where: online proctored or a Pearson VUE test center; results: within five business days, no pass or fail on screen). Every value cell is a fact link whose text holds the display. Then the trap list (D5 form, one line each) with the four traps placed here. Tie the domain row to her diagnostic in one plain sentence without a number (Secure is the largest share and her weakest domain).

sections.heading: Read the stem in this order
sections.plan: At most 300 words. Stem anatomy in one sentence: context, problem or change, zero to three constraints, then the ask with at most one capital qualifier (the book's own standard; method text). Then the reading order as a numbered list with bold step names: **Read the ask.** (the last sentence; find the capital word) **Mark the requirements.** (must, ensure, without, acceptable) **Predict before the options.** **Remove what breaks a requirement.** **Rank what is left on the qualifier.** **Answer every question.** Embed the diagram how-the-exam-asks-option-ladder after step 5. The instruction 'best complete the statement or answer the question' is quoted through exam-select-best-response-instruction; the definition of a distractor links exam-distractor-definition. Then the three reading traps placed here. The full list of the six distractor types is in 2-deep.md (Instruction grammar), not here.

sections.heading: Exam English core words
sections.plan: At most 450 words, hand text, no table (S2). Teach these twelve words of data/exam-english.json, each bold at first use, grouped in three short paragraphs: ranking words (ee-most-cost-effective, ee-least-operational-overhead, ee-most-secure, ee-capitalised-superlative), strength words (ee-must, ee-ensure, ee-acceptable, ee-wants-to-avoid), and the two words the exam guide itself pairs (ee-highly-available, ee-fault-tolerant), plus ee-which-solution and ee-these-requirements. Each word gets its plain meaning and what it signals, in the data file's own sense. The exam guide's own phrases are linked (exam-guide-cost-effective-wording, exam-guide-highly-available-fault-tolerant-wording). One closing paragraph for the stressed reader: the exam uses short service names and the full names are under the Help button (exam-short-service-names-help-button, exam-short-name-example), and some abbreviations are never expanded (exam-abbreviations-not-expanded). Place the two strength traps here.

sections.heading: Multiple-response questions
sections.plan: At most 200 words. The exam guide's rule (two or more correct responses out of five or more options, linked). Method: judge each option alone as true or false, then count your marks against the number in '(Select TWO.)' (ee-select-two); in 'Which combination of steps' (ee-which-combination) the chosen options must work together and not conflict. Do not state anything about partial credit (no AWS fact). Place the one trap here.

sections.heading: Check
sections.plan: Two prompts parallel to Predict, new cases (U4). Check 1: a stem asks for LEAST operational overhead; a script on an instance and a built-in feature of a managed service both work. Which ranks first, and why does the cheaper script not win? Reveal answers it and then '**Predict 1:**' in its own paragraph. Check 2: you run out of time with three questions unanswered. Should you guess? Reveal: no penalty for guessing, unanswered is scored as incorrect; then '**Predict 2:**' with 50 scored and 15 unscored that you cannot identify. Strict text: link every number and absolute word.

sections.heading: Recap from memory
sections.plan: Three prompts, answers hidden, each recalling only what 1-fast.md states (U4): Recap 1, the six reading steps in order; Recap 2, what MOST cost-effective asks for; Recap 3, the passing score and its scale.

sections.heading: The nine word groups
sections.plan: Nine H3, in file order of data/exam-english.json, heading = group title, time box 1 min each (sum 9). Each H3: one hand paragraph (60 to 100 words) that says what the group decides in a stem and which pair inside it is the classic twin, then the generated region <!-- exam-english:start group=<id> --> <!-- exam-english:end -->. A Go deeper reveal (at most 150 words) only where listed in the H3 plan. Hand words of the whole section 500 to 1200.

sections.heading: Optimisation qualifiers
sections.plan: The capital word ranks the options that already meet every requirement. The four domain names match four qualifiers (secure, resilient, high-performing, cost-optimized: exam-candidate-tasks). Twin to name: highly available against fault tolerant. Go deeper: the exam guide's own skill wording uses 'most cost-effective' and 'highly available and/or fault-tolerant' (link both wording facts), so the qualifiers are the guide's vocabulary, not exam trivia.

sections.heading: Workload shape
sections.plan: These words describe the load over time; they choose the pricing model and the scaling style. Twin to name: steady-state against unpredictable or spiky. Link the guide's 'stateless workloads compared with stateful workloads'. No Go deeper.

sections.heading: Strength of requirement
sections.plan: Hard words (must, mandates, ensure, stringent) remove options; soft words (acceptable, sufficient, at a minimum) open cheaper options. Twin to name: must against acceptable (the NAT gateway twins of the quiz turn on it). Method text only; the book's own modal rule (must = AWS requires it) applies to prose, while in a stem 'must' states the company's requirement. No Go deeper.

sections.heading: Data and time
sections.plan: These words set how fresh, how safe and how fast to reach the data must be. Twin to name: real-time against near real-time. Go deeper: RPO and RTO in AWS's own definitions (link both), and that the exam guide names them with the four DR strategies (exam-guide-disaster-recovery-rpo-rto-wording).

sections.heading: Operations
sections.plan: These words name work the team wants to give away. Twin to name: fully managed against provision. Link the guide's 'decoupling workloads so that components can scale independently' and, for 'patch', AWS's 'apply patches without requiring customer action' for multi-tenant managed services. No Go deeper.

sections.heading: Security
sections.plan: These words name who can reach what, and where the data is protected. Twin to name: at rest against in transit (the guide lists them as two skills: link). Note for her diagnostic: Secure is her weakest domain, so these ten words get one extra reading pass (plain sentence, no number). No Go deeper.

sections.heading: Location and network
sections.plan: These words say where users, data and traffic are. Twin to name: across multiple Availability Zones against cross-Region. Link the guide's 'global, hybrid, multi-tier' wording. Go deeper: Multi-AZ is part of a high availability strategy and DR strategies may also use multiple Regions (link), so read which failure the stem names: a zone or a Region.

sections.heading: Change and migration
sections.plan: These words set how much the application can change. Twin to name: without changing the application against minimal code changes. Link the guide's 'when application changes are not possible' and 'heterogeneous migrations, homogeneous migrations'. No Go deeper.

sections.heading: Instruction grammar
sections.plan: These phrases frame the question and tell you what kind of answer to give. Then the six distractor types as a short list in plain words (works but breaks the qualifier; a similar service; the right service configured wrongly; solves a different problem; a word from the stem and nothing else; a feature that does not exist), with the exam guide's own definition linked. Go deeper: a question that seems out of date (the newest-feature trap): a feature must be generally available for 3 months before it appears, AWS replaces impacted questions, and AWS says to choose the best available answer from the options (link all three). Place the trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-newest-feature-wins here.

sections.heading: Words customers say
sections.plan: At most 200 words, for listening in customer calls (STYLE 3): spin up, lift and shift, blast radius, noisy neighbour, guardrails, break-glass, cold start, landing zone. One list item each: the customer word, then the words the book and the exam use instead (launch; rehost; ...). Method text; no AWS fact claimed. lift-and-shift and blast-radius are terms of data/terms.json: bold at first use.

sections.heading: Confusable words
sections.plan: At most 200 words. Pairs, one list item each: highly available or fault tolerant; durable or available (availability is the percentage of time a workload is available for use: link); eventually ('after some time', not 'maybe': link the IAM eventual-consistency fact as the example); scale up or scale out; Multi-AZ or multi-Region; terminate or stop; principal or principle; route or root; affect or Effect. Place the three confusion traps here.

traps.belief: MOST cost-effective means the cheapest option is the answer.
traps.truth: The instruction asks for the response that best answers the question: an option that misses a stated requirement is a distractor at any price, and the qualifier ranks only the options that remain.

traps.belief: An option that repeats a word of the stem, such as 'privately', is probably the answer.
traps.truth: Distractors are generally plausible responses that match the content area, so a matching word decides nothing; check the option against every requirement.

traps.belief: If an option works, it is the answer.
traps.truth: A multiple-choice question has one correct response and three distractors, and the instruction asks for the best response; when several options work, the qualifier decides.

traps.belief: Leave a question blank when you are not sure, because a wrong guess costs points.
traps.truth: There is no penalty for guessing, and an unanswered question is scored as incorrect.

traps.belief: In a multiple-response question, pick the best option first and then the next-best one.
traps.truth: A multiple-response question has two or more correct responses out of five or more options, so judge each option on its own as correct or not.

traps.belief: You must pass each domain, such as Design Secure Architectures, to pass the exam.
traps.truth: The exam uses a compensatory scoring model: you need to pass only the overall exam.

traps.belief: A score of 720 means that 72 percent of the questions were correct.
traps.truth: Results are scaled scores from 100 to 1,000, not the raw number of correct questions, and AWS does not publish a raw passing count.

traps.belief: You can ask for ESL +30 after you book the exam, or on the test day.
traps.truth: ESL +30 is requested once, before you register for an exam, and it then applies to all future exam registrations.

traps.belief: The newest AWS feature is the right answer when it fits the stem.
traps.truth: A feature must be generally available for 3 months before it appears on an exam, and when a question seems affected by a change, you choose the best available answer from the options.

traps.belief: Highly available and fault tolerant name the same requirement.
traps.truth: The exam guide names them as two words ('highly available and/or fault-tolerant'); fault tolerant asks for no interruption, highly available accepts a short one.
'Eventually' means after some time: an eventually consistent change takes some time to reach every reader.

traps.belief: A Multi-AZ design also protects against the failure of a whole Region.
traps.truth: Multiple Availability Zones are part of a high availability strategy; DR strategies may also use multiple Regions.

traps.belief: The right design is the most available one, even when the stem accepts an interruption.
traps.truth: AWS names the trade-off: a development environment can reduce cost at the expense of reliability, and a multi-Region design where a multi-AZ design meets the requirements is an anti-pattern.

traps.belief: A control that detects the action and sends an alert meets an 'ensure' or 'prevent' requirement.
traps.truth: 'Ensure' and 'prevent' ask for a control that stops the action, and the strongest actor in the stem must be stopped too: an SCP restricts users and roles in member accounts, including the member account's root user.

question_slots.lesson: Read which failure the stem names (one Availability Zone) and choose the design that survives exactly that failure.
question_slots.misconception_plan: a larger instance in one Availability Zone (scale up is not availability); daily snapshots (a backup is not availability); Auto Scaling inside one Availability Zone

question_slots.lesson: Strict twin A. The phrase 'an interruption of internet access is acceptable if one Availability Zone fails' opens the cheaper design.
question_slots.twin: strict twin of slot 6: the stems differ in one phrase only, the four options are identical, the key moves. Shared stem: workloads in private subnets in three Availability Zones download operating system updates through NAT; the instances must not have public IP addresses; traffic volume is small (say so, so that cross-AZ data transfer does not decide the cost). Phrase here: 'If one Availability Zone fails, an interruption of internet access is acceptable.' Key: one NAT gateway in one public subnet, used by every private route table. Options (neutral words): one NAT gateway shared by all zones; one NAT gateway in each zone, each private route table to the gateway in its own zone; a gateway VPC endpoint (different problem: updates come from the internet); public IP addresses and an internet gateway route (breaks the no-public-IP requirement). Do not offer a NAT instance: no fact ranks its cost.

question_slots.lesson: Several options work; the qualifier ranks them. IAM users in every account work but cost the most effort.
question_slots.misconception_plan: IAM users with the same name in each account (works, violates the qualifier); one shared IAM user with a password (breaks least privilege); a script that copies policies to each account

question_slots.lesson: Strict twin A, worked (wrong_path false). 'Privately' is a requirement both endpoint types meet; the cost qualifier then picks the endpoint with no hourly or processing charge.
question_slots.twin: strict twin of slot 8. Shared stem: EC2 instances in private subnets currently send large uploads to an S3 bucket in the same Region through a NAT gateway; the traffic must stay off the public internet; the company wants to cut the NAT gateway data processing charge. Phrase here: 'The uploads come only from the instances in the VPC.' Key: a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 with routes in the private route tables. Options (identical in both twins): gateway endpoint; interface endpoint for S3 in each Availability Zone; a second NAT gateway in another zone; public subnets with public IP addresses (breaks the requirement).

worked.note: think-aloud: I read the ask (MOST cost-effectively), mark 'stay off the public internet' and 'only from the instances in the VPC', predict a gateway endpoint, remove the public-subnet option, then rank the two endpoints on cost.

question_slots.lesson: 'A small team' plus LEAST operational overhead: the managed device wins over the device you patch, even if the other works.
question_slots.misconception_plan: NAT instance with a failover script (works, violates the qualifier; managed by you, including patches); internet gateway and public IP addresses (breaks a stated no-public-IP requirement); gateway VPC endpoint (solves a different problem)

question_slots.lesson: Strict twin B. 'Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails' removes the cheaper shared design before the qualifier ranks.
question_slots.twin: strict twin of slot 2 (twin_of slot 2's question id; at least 3 questions between them). Phrase here: 'Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails.' Key: one NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, each private route table to the gateway in its own zone. Options identical to slot 2.

question_slots.lesson: Multiple response, 'Which combination of steps ... (Select TWO.)': each chosen step is correct on its own and the two work together. Correct pair: create an IAM role with a least-privilege policy for the bucket, and attach the role to the instances through an instance profile and delete the stored keys.
question_slots.misconception_plan: rotate the access keys with a scheduled script (works, violates the qualifier and the mandate); store the keys in environment variables (still long-term keys); create one IAM user per instance; give the role AdministratorAccess (breaks least privilege)

question_slots.lesson: Strict twin B, worked with a wrong path. The cheapest endpoint fails one requirement (traffic from the data center), so the cost qualifier ranks only what is left.
question_slots.twin: strict twin of slot 4 (twin_of slot 4's question id). Phrase here: 'The uploads also come from servers in the company's data center over AWS Direct Connect.' Key: an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Options identical to slot 4.

worked.note: step 3 predicts the gateway endpoint because it has no charge; step 5 says 'My first idea breaks because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks', then picks the interface endpoint.

question_slots.lesson: A 'must not' or 'without' requirement removes options before anything else: no inbound SSH from the internet, and every session recorded.
question_slots.misconception_plan: a bastion host with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 (breaks the stated requirement); a security group rule for port 22 from the internet on each instance; a network ACL that allows port 22

question_slots.lesson: Two requirements, two steps: each correct option meets one requirement on its own (a network ACL deny rule for the range; a web security group that allows HTTPS only from the load balancer's security group).
question_slots.misconception_plan: a deny rule in the security group (impossible feature: security groups hold allow rules only; link the fact in its why); host firewall software on every instance with a maintained deny list (works, violates the qualifier); a security group rule that allows HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0

question_slots.lesson: 'Ensure that no one in the member accounts, including the root user, can ...' asks for prevention that reaches the strongest actor: an SCP, not a detection or an IAM policy.
question_slots.misconception_plan: an alert when the action happens (detects, does not prevent); an identity-based deny policy on every user and role (cannot reach the root user: iam-root-user-no-identity-policies-or-boundary); a permissions boundary on every role (same gap)

question_slots.lesson: The stem names the failure of one Availability Zone. A second Region also survives it, but costs more than the requirement asks: the qualifier removes it.
question_slots.misconception_plan: copy the stack to a second Region (works, violates the qualifier; multi-Region where multi-AZ suffices is an anti-pattern); a larger instance in one zone (different problem); one NAT gateway shared by both zones (wrong configuration: the other zone loses internet access)

twin_pairs.changed_phrase: an interruption is acceptable / must continue
only from the instances in the VPC / also from the data center over Direct Connect

question_plan.file_order: write the items in slot order 1 to 12; the two worked questions print first in 5-quiz.md by the tool (S2). Keep at least 3 questions between twins (slots 2 and 6; 4 and 8).
rules_for_the_writer: Each question teaches a reading move: its explanation names the deciding phrase (keywords) and the lesson of its slot; the AWS mechanism is linked, never taught at length.
Stems say 'A company', never Callvale. Allowed: negative stems (allow_negative_stems), but no slot needs one.
Topics include 'start' plus the domain topic (networking, identity, security, resilience, cost).
The key never rests on a volatile fact (no regional NAT gateway, no price example, no 2024 public IPv4 charge).
Slot 2: state that the traffic volume is small, so that the cross-AZ data transfer charge of a shared NAT gateway does not compete with the hourly charge of three gateways.
Slot 9: do not offer EC2 Instance Connect as an option (it would be a second defensible answer).

term_requests: qualifier (the one capital word, MOST or LEAST and so on, that ranks the options that work)
distractor (exam guide: an incorrect response that a candidate with incomplete knowledge might choose)
stem (the scenario and the question, before the options)
multiple response (a question with two or more correct responses)
tasks_note: No task. The front template allows at most one Try, and no AWS action teaches reading a stem; the practice for this chapter is the quiz and the web app's stem-first mode. No IAM user, no resource, no cost.
cards_note: The template counts 0 written cards. The 90 `word` cards (deck exam-english) are generated by `cards build --only words` from data/exam-english.json into data/01-how-the-exam-asks/cards.json; nobody writes them by hand. English only.

diagrams.title: Which option survives?
diagrams.claim: An option is the answer when it meets every requirement and ranks first on the qualifier.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with three questions that you ask of each option. First: does it break a stated requirement? Yes removes it. Second: does it solve a different problem? Yes removes it. Third: does another working option rank higher on the qualifier? Yes removes it. An option that passes all three questions is the answer.

rungs.q: Does it break a stated requirement?
Does it solve a different problem?
Does another working option rank higher?

diagrams.notes: Method picture, no AWS fact. The claim and alt hold no absolute word and no number with a unit, so they need no fact link (L705). A ladder returns no numbered steps, so `say` is empty.
